Cav Order

1. This is an owner's appeal under section 173 of the Motor Vehicles Act challenging the award dated 22.02.2016 passed by Additional Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Katghora, District Korba (CG) in Motor Accident Claim Case No.26/2011 awarding compensation of Rs.5,02,000/- with interest @
7% per annum, from the date of application till its realization, in favour of the claimants and against the appellant.

entities.text: Additional Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Katghora, District Korba
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: 2. The gist of claim before the Tribunal, in brief, was that on 20.03.2010, deceased Sahnawaz was going from Renpur to Deepka on a motorcycle with his friend Sumeshgiri Goswami.

At about 2-3 p.m., respondent No.3 Saddam Hussain while driving the offending vehicle i.e. Trailer bearing registration No.CG 10 CO 2890 rashly and negligently dashed his motorcycle ahead of Nehru Nagar Batari, as a result of which, Sahnawaj suffered grievous injuries and died on the spot.

The claimants,
who are the mother and brother of the deceased, preferred an application before the Claims Tribunal claiming compensation of Rs.38,70,000/-.

Learned Tribunal, on a close scrutiny of the evidence available on record, awarded total compensation of Rs.5,02,000/- in favour of the claimants with interest @ 7% per annum, from the date of application till its realization.

While passing the impugned award, the Tribunal has saddled the liability of payment of compensation upon the owner of the offending vehicle against which the present appeal has been filed by the owner.
The finding of the Tribunal is in accordance with Para-9 of the award wherein violation of insurance policy has been found as the driver was not found to have valid and effective licence.

3. Learned counsel for appellant has argued that the appellant- registered owner of the offending vehicle had exercised due care in appointing Saddam Hussain as the driver of the offending vehicle who had a valid and effective driving license.
The Insurance Company has not been able to prove the negligence on the part of the owner in appointing the driver.
In such a situation, the finding of the Tribunal regarding violation of insurance conditions is erroneous and cannot be sustained.

Therefore, the appeal should be allowed, the owner should be exonerated from the liability and the award amount should be recovered from the Insurance Company as it is undisputed that the offending vehicle was insured by the insurance company.

In support of his argument, learned counsel for appellant relied upon the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the cases of Nirmala Kothari v. United India Insurance Company Limited, (2020) 4 SCC 49 & Pepsu Road Transport Corporation v. National Insurance Company, (2013) 10 SCC 217.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Learned counsel for respondent No.4 Insurance Company argues that the registered owner of the offending vehicle neither gave any details of the valid driving licence of the driver in his written statement nor did he come before the Court with clean hands.
No licence of the driver has been produced on record on his behalf.
The driver himself or the registered owner did not even come to the witness box.

Thus, their bona fides have not been shown and in the absence of which, it cannot be assumed that the registered owner had taken sufficient care at the time of appointing driver Saddam Hussain as the driver of the offending vehicle to ensure that Saddam Hussain is a valid and effective driving licence holder.
Therefore, the finding of the Tribunal is justified, the argument of the appellant is not acceptable and the appeal may be dismissed.

5. Heard learned counsel appearing for the parties and perused the record with utmost circumspection.
6.
From perusal of the record it is clear that no evidence has been presented by the driver and the registered owner of the offending vehicle.
No written statement was produced by the driver of the offending vehicle Saddam Hussain.
In the written statement of the appellant i.e. the registered owner of the offending vehicle, no details of the driving license of driver Saddam Hussain have been mentioned.

It has only been stated that after looking at the driver's license, he had appointed him as his driver and the driver had a valid and effective license.
7.
On the other hand, the alleged driving licence of Saddam Hussain which was seized in the criminal case has been exhibited by the claimant side as Ex.P-4.

The Assistant Manager of the insurance company Sandeep Kumar Sinha has been examined on behalf of the insurance company who has stated that the alleged driving licence No. S/2068/07 in the name of Saddam Hussain,
which is exhibited as Ex.P-4, was not found to have been issued by the Regional Transport Office,
Raipur.

In this regard, the Tribunal had issued commission and got the Assistant Grade-2 R. K.
Khalkho of the Regional Transport Office, Raipur examined, who in his statement has stated that as per the office records, on 24/03/2007 (as mentioned in Exhibit P-4), no driving licence was issued from his office in the name of Saddam Hussain.
Thus, the driving licence Exhibit P-4 was not found to have been issued by the Regional Transport Office, Raipur.
Therefore, the conclusion given by the Tribunal regarding the said driving license being fake is justified and does not require any interference.

8. In the case of Nirmala Kothari (Supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Para-9, 10 & 12 held as under:
"Having set forth the facts of the present case, the question of law that arises for consideration is what is the extent of care/diligence expected of the employer/insured while employing a driver?
To answer this question, we shall advert to the legal position regarding the liability of the Insurance Company when the driver of the offending vehicle possessed an invalid/fake driving licence.
In the case of United India Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Lehru & Ors.

a two Judge Bench of this court has taken the view that the Insurance Company cannot be permitted to avoid its liability on the ground that the person driving the vehicle at the time of the accident was not M/S Hind Energy And Coal Beneficiation ... vs Smt. sentences.text: It was further held that the willful breach of the conditions of the policy should be established.
The law with this respect has been discussed in detail in the case of Pepsu RTC vs. National Insurance Co.

entities.text: Pepsu RTC vs. National Insurance Co.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: We may extract the relevant paragraph from the Judgment: (Pepsu case, (2013) 10 SCC p. 223, para 10) "10.
In a claim for compensation, it is certainly open to the insurer under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) to take a defence that the driver of the vehicle involved in the accident was not duly licensed.
Once such a defence is taken, the onus is on the insurer.
But even after it is proved that the licence possessed by the driver was a fake one, whether there is liability on the insurer is the moot question.
As far as the owner of the vehicle is concerned, when he hires a driver, he has to check whether the driver has a valid driving licence.
Thereafter he has to satisfy himself as to the competence of the driver.
If satisfied in that regard also, it can be said that the owner had taken reasonable care in employing a person who is qualified and competent to drive the vehicle.
The owner cannot be expected to go beyond that, to the extent of verifying the genuineness of the driving licence with the licensing authority before hiring the services of the driver.

However, the situation would be different if at the time of insurance of the vehicle or thereafter the insurance company requires the owner of the vehicle to have the licence duly verified from the licensing authority or if the attention of the owner of the vehicle is otherwise invited to the allegation that the licence issued to the driver employed by him is a fake one and yet the owner does not take appropriate action for verification of the matter regarding the genuineness of the licence from the licensing authority.
That is what is explained in Swaran Singh's case (supra).

If despite such information with the owner that the licence possessed by his driver is fake, no action is taken by the insured for appropriate verification, then the insured will be at fault and, in such circumstances, the insurance company is not liable for the compensation."

10. While the insurer can certainly take the defence that the licence of the driver of the car at the time of accident was invalid/fake however the onus of proving that the insured did not take adequate care and caution to verify the genuineness of the licence or was guilty of willful breach of the conditions of the insurance policy or the contract of insurance lies on the insurer.
12. While hiring a driver the employer is expected to verify if the driver has a driving licence.

If the driver produces a licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the employer is not expected to further investigate into the authenticity of the licence unless there is cause to believe otherwise.

If the employer finds the driver to be competent to drive the vehicle and has satisfied himself that the driver has a driving licence there would be no breach of 149(2)(a)(ii) and the Insurance Company would be liable under the policy.
It would be unreasonable to place such a high onus on the insured to make enquiries with RTOs all over the country to ascertain the veracity of the driving licence.

However, if the Insurance Company is able to prove that the owner/insured was aware or had notice that the licence was fake or invalid and still permitted the person to drive, the insurance company would no longer continue to be liable."

sentences.text:
The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in the matter of Pappu and Others Vs. Vinod Kumar Lamba and Another reported in 2018 (3) SCC. 208, in paragraphs-12 & 13, in respect of the burden of proof regarding a valid license, has held as follows:
"12.

entities.text: Pappu and Others Vs. Vinod Kumar Lamba and Another reported in 2018 (3) SCC. 208
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
This Court in the case of National Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Swaran Singh and Ors.,
(2004) 3 SCC 297, has noticed the defences available to the Insurance Company under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) of the Motor Vehi- cles Act, 1988.

entities.text:
National Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Swaran Singh and Ors.,
(2004) 3 SCC 297
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Insurance Company is entitled to take a defence that the offending vehicle was driven by an unauthorised person or the person driving the vehi- cle did not have a valid driving licence.

The onus would shift on the Insurance Company only after the owner of the offending vehicle pleads and proves the basic facts within his knowledge that the driver of the offending ve- hicle was authorised by him to drive the vehicle and was having a valid driving licence at the relevant time.

13. In the present case, the respondent No.1 owner of the offending vehicle merely raised a vague plea in the Written Statement that the offending vehicle DIL-5955 was being driven by a person having valid driving licence.
He did not disclose the name of the driver and his other details.
Besides, the respondent No.1 did not enter the witness box or examine any witness in support of this plea.

The respondent No.2 Insurance Company in the Written Statement has plainly refuted that plea and also asserted that the offending vehicle was not driven by an authorised person and having valid driving licence.

The respondent No.1 owner of the offending vehicle did not produce any evidence except a driving licence of one Joginder Singh, without any specific stand taken in the pleadings or in the evidence that the same Joginder Singh was, in fact, authorised to drive the vehicle in question at the relevant time.
Only then would onus shift, requiring the respondent No.2 Insurance Company to rebut such evidence and to produce other evidence to substantiate its defence.

Merely producing a valid insurance certificate in respect of the offending Truck was not enough for the respondent No.1 to make the Insurance Company liable to discharge his liability arising from rash and negligent driving by the driver of his vehicle.

The Insurance Company can be fastened with the liability on the basis of a valid insurance policy only after the basic facts are pleaded and established by the owner of the offending vehicle - that the vehicle was not only duly insured but also that it was driven by an authorised person having a valid driving licence.

Without disclosing the name of the driver in the Written Statement or producing any evidence to substantiate the fact that the copy of the driving licence produced in support was of a person who, in fact,
was authorised to drive the offending vehicle at the relevant time, the owner of the vehicle cannot be said to have extricated himself from his liability.

The Insurance Company would become liable only after such foundational facts are pleaded and proved by the owner of the offending vehicle."
10.

In the light of the above judgments and keeping in view the pleadings and evidence presented on record, it is clear that no details the driver's license were given on behalf of the appellant - registered owner of the offending vehicle but a vague statement was made that he had appointed the driver M/S Hind Energy And Coal Beneficiation ... vs Smt. Hasina Khatun on 4 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/90796194/
5 after seeing and finding his licence valid.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It cannot be said that the appellant - registered owner came before the Tribunal with clean hands by not giving details of the driver's license in his written statement.
No driving license of driver Saddam Hussain has been produced on record by the owner.
When the claimant party presented the seized driving license as Ex.P-4, the insurance company called evidence and proved that the said license was fake.

Thus, from the evidence, it is clear that the appellant - registered owner, in discharging his primary burden of proof, has neither given the details of the driving licence by making a clear statement nor produced the driving license on seeing which he claimed to have appointed the driver, nor did the registered owner or the driver come in the witness box to establish his bona fides or establish the fact that he was not negligent at the time of appointing the driver.

Therefore, in the light the aforesaid judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, this Court is of the opinion that the conclusion of the Tribunal exonerating the insurance company from its liability by finding violation of the insurance conditions is justified and does not call for any interference.
11. The appellant - registered owner is a company which is fully resourced and financially capable of paying compensation.
In such a situation, it is not found appropriate and necessary to pass an order of pay and recover in this case.
12. Hence, the appeal is dismissed.
13. Records of the Tribunal along with a copy of this order be sent back forthwith for compliance and necessary action, if any.

Sd/-
